title: Why Are We So Groupish?
coreMove: Hold selfish motives and group-binding motives in the same picture instead of reducing one to the other.
sourcePressure: The chapter reopens morality through groupishness, multilevel selection, and the tension between self-interest and group-binding tendencies.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer reduces groupishness to mob thinking and misses the self-interest versus group-binding tension.

sourceAnchors.name: multilevel selection
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar identifies multilevel selection as the chapter-level frame for selfishness and groupishness.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Multilevel selection gives the reader a way to hold two facts together: people compete as individuals and bind into groups.

sourceAnchors.name: the shift into Part III
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen sidecar says the book shifts here from partisan moral foundations into the social and evolutionary logic of group life.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The moral question gets bigger here; it is no longer only what a person judges, but what a group can become.

hook: Do not open ch09 with a person discovering that morality is complicated.
Do not use 'you think X, but actually Y' as the hook shell.
counterintuition: Avoid treating the opposing view as stupid before explaining the mechanism.
tryThisNow: No generic write down your values prompt.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: volunteer fire brigade deciding who gets scarce training slots
exampleSpecs.audience: volunteers balancing ambition and crew loyalty
exampleSpecs.stakes: Olivia holds individual advancement and brigade readiness together.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Olivia moves one name down the list because the crew needs a pump operator more than another captain.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Mud from last night's call dries on the firehouse floor beneath the roster.

exampleSpecs.audience: software contributors who mistake all conflict for ego
exampleSpecs.stakes: Mikkel sees individual credit and group survival pulling at once.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Mikkel asks the contributor what would help the project live after the contributor leaves.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Do you want the patch merged, or the project healthier?" Mikkel asks.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Adaeze notices when self-protection turns into block-level protection.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Adaeze watches residents stop counting their own sandbags and start filling the weakest corner.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Wet sand sticks to Adaeze's wrists as the river climbs the curb.

exampleSpecs.domain: academic department deciding whether to share grant credit
exampleSpecs.audience: researchers balancing status and lab survival
exampleSpecs.stakes: Jack frames credit as individual incentive and group resource.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 4:05, Jack redraws the authorship chart to protect both contribution and lab continuity.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 4:05, Jack stands before an authorship chart no one wants to touch.

exampleSpecs.domain: local choir choosing dues for members who cannot pay
exampleSpecs.stakes: Kasia names the moment the choir pays a cost to remain a choir.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Kasia ask what kind of group they become if the best alto leaves over dues.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You hear the alto part missing before anyone discusses money.

exampleSpecs.domain: cycling club enforcing safety norms on a popular rider
exampleSpecs.audience: club leaders facing status versus group welfare
exampleSpecs.stakes: Antoine treats the rider's talent and the group's safety as competing levels.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Antoine reviews the near miss and suspends the rider for the group's future rides.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Antoine one helmet-camera clip to stop calling it a personality clash.

skillTargets: hold individual and group-level incentives together
recognize group-binding motives without romanticizing them
use multilevel selection as a frame rather than a settled slogan

tryThisNowSpec: Think of one group you sacrifice for and one you merely use; write the cue that makes the difference visible.
